questions.question: What does `re.match()` check that `re.search()` does not?
options: match() only checks whether the pattern occurs at the very start of the string; search() checks the whole string for a match anywhere.
match() is case-insensitive by default.
match() only works with compiled patterns.
match() returns a list of all matches; search() returns just one.
questions.explanation: re.match() anchors to the beginning of the string, so a pattern that clearly appears later in the string but not at position 0 will not match — re.search() checks anywhere in the string.

questions.question: What does the pattern `\d+` match?
options: Exactly one digit.
Any single character at all.
One or more digits.
Zero or more digits.
questions.explanation: \d matches a single digit character; + means 'one or more of the previous element', so \d+ matches a run of one or more digits.

questions.question: What does a capturing group `()` let you do?
options: Make that part of the pattern optional.
Repeat that part of the pattern automatically.
Ignore that part of the pattern during matching.
Retrieve just that part of the match afterward via .group(n), instead of re-parsing the whole match yourself.
questions.explanation: A parenthesized group is captured separately from the overall match, retrievable individually — e.g. group(1) for the first group — without needing to slice or re-parse the full matched text.

questions.question: What is the advantage of a named group `(?P<year>\d{4})` over a numbered group `(\d{4})`?
options: Named groups match faster than numbered groups.
Named groups are retrieved by a descriptive name (.group('year') or .groupdict()), which stays correct even if you reorder groups later.
Named groups can match multiple different values simultaneously.
There is no real difference between the two.
questions.explanation: Numbered groups (.group(1), .group(2)) become fragile and hard to read as a pattern grows; named groups are self-documenting and remain correct if the group order in the pattern changes.

questions.question: What does `re.sub(pattern, replacement, text)` do?
options: Replaces every match of pattern in text with replacement (a string or a function).
Splits text into pieces wherever pattern matches.
Removes pattern from text without putting anything in its place.
Counts how many times pattern occurs in text.
questions.explanation: re.sub performs search-and-replace across every match of pattern in text; the replacement can be a plain string or a function called once per match.

questions.question: What is the difference between the greedy quantifier `.*` and the lazy quantifier `.*?`?
options: There is no difference; they always match identical text.
Lazy quantifiers are always faster to execute than greedy ones.
Greedy quantifiers only work inside re.findall, never re.search.
Greedy matches as much as possible; lazy matches as little as possible — this changes the result whenever there are multiple possible stopping points.
questions.explanation: Given text with more than one matching delimiter, .* consumes as much as possible before backtracking to satisfy the rest of the pattern, while .*? stops at the very first opportunity — producing very different results on the same input.

questions.question: Why should regex patterns almost always be written as raw strings (`r'...'`)?
options: Raw strings execute faster at runtime.
Without the r prefix, Python's own string escaping (e.g. \n as newline) can collide with regex escaping (e.g. \d), causing confusing bugs.
The re module raises a SyntaxError on non-raw pattern strings.
Raw strings automatically make the match case-insensitive.
questions.explanation: A pattern like '\d' (no r prefix) risks Python interpreting backslash sequences itself before the regex engine ever sees the string; r'\d' passes the two characters through unambiguously.

questions.question: What does `re.compile(pattern)` give you that calling `re.search(pattern, text)` directly does not?
options: Automatic case-insensitivity.
The ability to reuse the pre-parsed pattern object across many searches without re-parsing the pattern string each time.
The ability to match nested structures like HTML or JSON.
A guarantee that the pattern will only ever match once.
questions.explanation: Compiling a pattern once and reusing the resulting object (especially inside a loop) avoids re-parsing the same pattern string on every call, and is clearer when the same pattern is used repeatedly.

questions.question: Why is regex generally a poor tool for parsing deeply nested structures like HTML or JSON?
options: Regex cannot use character classes like [A-Za-z].
Regex only works on ASCII text, not Unicode.
Regex can only match a fixed, predetermined number of characters.
Regex has no built-in concept of nesting depth or balanced structure — a real parser is the correct tool for that.
questions.explanation: Regex matches flat patterns of characters; it cannot track how many levels deep a tag or bracket is nested, which is exactly what parsing nested structures correctly requires — that's a job for a real parser, not a bigger pattern.

questions.question: What does the word-boundary anchor `\b` match?
options: Any whitespace character.
A line break specifically.
The literal two-character sequence backslash-b.
The invisible edge between a word character and a non-word character (or the start/end of the string), consuming no characters itself.
questions.explanation: \b is a zero-width assertion — it matches a position, not a character, at the boundary between \w (word) and non-\w characters, which is why \b[a-z]+\b matches whole words rather than partial ones.
